output:
**The one assignment**

Jess texted me last night: “It’s one assignment. Don’t torch your job over it.”

I know she meant it kindly. Half the group chat agreed with her, which is probably why I’m writing this instead of sending sixteen increasingly defensive texts. I’m not mad at Jess. I get why she said it. I’d just rather explain myself once, properly, and let everybody decide what they think.

For four years, I’ve assigned the same project to my two sections of juniors in US History II at Cobb Street High. They interview someone in their family or neighborhood about Boston’s busing and desegregation crisis of 1974–76, then turn in a ten-minute recording and a two-page reflection. The textbook gives the story one paragraph. The project asks students to hear it from somebody who lived it.

Until now, nobody has complained.

This time, a parent emailed Dr. Halvorsen, our principal, and copied a school committee member. The parent said the project “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.” On Thursday, November 19, at 3:15, I’ll meet with Dr. Halvorsen and the parent.

I don’t think the parent is just looking for a fight. I think there’s a real point underneath the complaint. Asking a kid to interview a relative about something painful can put them in a strange position. They may hear something they weren’t ready for, or feel like they’re supposed to approve or condemn someone they love. That’s a lot to put on a teenager. I don’t want to pretend otherwise.

So I’m changing the assignment. I’ll add an alternative: students can interview a librarian or archivist, or work with recordings from previous years, with permission. No one has to interview a family member. The project stays, but the pressure to go home and ask a personal question does not.

That seems like a reasonable line to draw. I don’t get to force anyone to have a hard conversation. I do think students deserve the chance to understand the history of the city they live in.

In 2023, a student I’ll call D. interviewed his grandmother. She had driven a school bus in Southie in 1974 and, as far as he knew, had never told anyone in the family about it. He played about forty seconds of the interview for the class. Then nobody said anything for nearly a minute.

Not because I had asked them to be solemn. Nobody needed to tell them what to do. They were listening.

Last year, one student found out her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was upset. We talked after class twice. I’m not going to turn that into a neat story about a project changing her life. She was upset, and the conversation was difficult. Her reflection was also the best thing I read all year. Both things can be true.

The uncomfortable parts aren’t automatically the useful parts. A kid being distressed isn’t proof that the assignment is working. But discomfort can be part of learning, especially when the history is close enough to reach into your own family or neighborhood. The kids who feel uncomfortable may be the ones who need the opportunity most. “Opportunity” matters there: it is not an obligation.

Jess and I met while student teaching at the same school in 2012. She left teaching in 2019 and now works in HR at a biotech in Cambridge. She knows me well enough to know that I can get stuck on the principle of a thing and forget that there are practical consequences. She’s right that I could get burned.

I’m tenured. I’ve been tenured since 2021. That doesn’t mean I can’t make my working life harder. Dr. Halvorsen still controls my schedule and who gets AP. I’m not so secure that I can pretend those things don’t matter. And I’m scared, a little. Not in a brave, standing-on-a-desk kind of way. More in the ordinary way where you wonder whether you’re being stubborn and whether this meeting could have been avoided if you’d just picked an easier assignment.

But I don’t think dropping the project is the right answer. I think making it less coercive is.

I’m not trying to pick a fight with the parent, or win one with my principal. I want students to have a way into a part of Boston’s history that the textbook barely makes room for. And I want them to have a way out of the interview-with-family part if that’s not right for them. That’s the whole thing, really: the history matters, and the kid gets a choice.

Jess doesn’t have to agree with me. I mostly want her to understand why I’m not letting this one go.

I’ll text her after the meeting Thursday. Hopefully with boring news. And either way, I’ll tell her I’m glad she said something, even if I needed more than one text to answer.

reasons: The piece says 'sixteen increasingly defensive texts', but the request says the writer wanted to avoid arguing in 'fifteen texts', so the number is changed.
